name: Cantharidin solution

lead: Cantharidin is a blistering compound from blister beetles. Dermatologists apply it to molluscum bumps and warts so a blister lifts the lesion away.
The FDA approved the Ycanth formulation for molluscum in July 2023.

paras: It causes a controlled blister in the skin layer holding the lesion; the blister heals and the lesion goes with it, reportedly without scarring.
Pain, blisters and chemical burns can occur on skin. Swallowing it can cause serious kidney and gut damage. It is prescription and clinician-applied.

chain: Cantharidin applied to lesions by a clinician
Blister forms and lifts the lesion
angle.text: A clinician paints the solution on molluscum bumps or warts, a blister forms and the lesion lifts away, typically healing without scarring. People seek it to clear visible bumps cosmetically and avoid scraping or freezing.

lead: Cantharidin is a blistering agent made by blister beetles that dermatologists apply to skin to remove molluscum contagiosum bumps and warts.[1][2] It helps looks by clearing visible lesions on the face, hands, feet or body, and the blister-and-lift approach is reported to heal without scarring.[1] A prescription topical, Ycanth (cantharidin 0.7%, VP-102), was approved by the FDA in July 2023 for molluscum contagiosum in people aged 2 and older.[1][3]

Cantharidin was first isolated in 1810 by the French chemist Pierre Robiquet from the beetles once sold as Spanish fly.[1] Its use against warts was studied by 1958.[1] Phase 3 trials of VP-102 in molluscum enrolled over 500 people, and phase 2 trials examined common and genital warts.[4][5][2][6]
Cantharidin is applied only by a clinician. It is a potent vesicant and is toxic if swallowed, so over-the-counter sale is illegal in many countries.[1]

paras: Approved use is treatment of molluscum contagiosum in patients aged 2 and older.[1][7] Dilute solutions have also been used for common warts, and VP-102 has been tested on genital warts.[1][8] A 2024 review describes three liquid forms: Ycanth (0.7%), Canthacur (0.7%) and Canthacur PS, a combination of 1% cantharidin, 30% salicylic acid and 2% podophyllotoxin indicated for plantar warts only. It reports a good-to-excellent response for molluscum, plantar warts and common warts, and mixed results for anogenital warts.[3]

Molluscum lesions often clear by themselves in six to twelve months, and people who treat them do so for cosmetic reasons or to prevent spread.[9] Wikipedia also records cantharidin solutions being used to remove tattoos.[1]

Cantharidin is absorbed by the lipid membranes of epidermal cells and triggers release of serine proteases. These enzymes break down desmosomal plaques, so cells lose their attachments (acantholysis) and a blister forms; Wikipedia states that lesions heal without scarring.[1] A 2023 review of Ycanth describes the same mechanism as promoting shedding of infected cells and viral clearance.[6]
Wikipedia gives the chemical formula as C10H12O4 and describes an odorless, colourless terpenoid with a bridged tricyclic structure.[1]

Two phase 3 randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials (CAMP-1 and CAMP-2, about 266 and 262 participants) tested VP-102, a drug-device combination of 0.7% cantharidin with gentian violet, acetone and denatonium benzoate, applied once every 21 days until the lesions cleared or for up to four treatments. At day 84, complete clearance was reported in 46 percent (73 of 160) on VP-102 versus 18 percent (19 of 106) on vehicle in CAMP-1, and 54 percent (81 of 150) versus 13 percent (15 of 112) in CAMP-2. Common adverse events were mild to moderate and included application-site reactions, itching and pain.[6][4][5]

A phase 2 trial of 56 patients examined cantharidin with occlusion on common warts, and a 105-patient placebo-controlled phase 2 study tested VP-102 on external genital warts.[2][8] Cantharidin-induced blisters are also used as a research model of skin inflammation in healthy volunteers.[10]

Topical effects include pain, itching and blistering, and severe chemical burns can occur.[1][6][9] The 2024 review reports mild and transient adverse events overall.[3] Swallowing cantharidin can cause serious gastrointestinal and kidney damage and is fatal at high doses; Wikipedia gives fatal oral doses recorded in the tens of milligrams.[1]

Blister-beetle preparations known as Spanish fly were used for centuries as aphrodisiacs and irritants, sometimes with fatal results, and were also used historically against smallpox.[1] Robiquet isolated the pure compound in 1810.[1] Through the twentieth century dermatologists used dilute cantharidin preparations for warts, and Verrica Pharmaceuticals developed a standardised version, Ycanth, which in 2023 became the first FDA-approved molluscum treatment.[1][7]

Cantharidin is prescription-only in the United States and is classed as an extremely hazardous substance; in New Zealand it is Class A under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, and in many countries sale or use without a prescription is illegal.[1] Ycanth is marketed by Verrica Pharmaceuticals.[1][7]
